supplement.where: Internal appendices: Appendix A starts on PDF p. 47; Appendix B starts on PDF p. 66 and ends on p. 72. Appendix A figures also float onto pp. 67-68. No separate supplement URL is stated.
supplement.holds: Table 12 (p. 47): semantic-similarity coefficients and standard errors; Table 14 (p. 49): mean, language-interaction, and median word-count regressions; Table 15 (p. 50): nonrandomized editing comparison; Table 21 (p. 56): arm means, SDs, and post counts; Figures 13-14 (pp. 65, 67): embedding visualizations; Figure 15 (p. 68): randomized roll-out outcomes; Appendix B (pp. 66, 69-72): returning-employer experiment. Footnote 27 (p. 47) promises example posts in A.8, but the saved appendix contains no such examples.

paper_design_summary: A platform randomized newly registered employer accounts to an optional AI-written first draft of a real job post or its standard posting flow, and measured similarity and length of the published text. The paper also reports a randomized experiment among returning employers and a later randomized roll-out to new employers. The editing comparison is a nonrandomized analysis of the main experiment's treated sample; the employer-account counts do not establish the number of distinct people analyzed.

studies.label: Main field experiment: AI-written first drafts for new employers (June 7 to July 20, 2023)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Employer-account assignment to an offer of an AI-written first job-post draft versus the standard posting flow. Assignment persists across later attempts. Uptake is optional; text outcomes condition on publishing a post, so they are not full-sample intention-to-treat outcomes.
assignment.quote: From June 07, 2023, through July 20, 2023, new employers on the platform were randomly allocated to either the status quo control experience or the treated experience.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9, Sections 3 and 3.1; p. 24, Section 6

arms.name: Treatment (AI draft offered)
arms.description: Optional AI-generated first draft, skills list, and category from a short employer prompt; editable before posting with optional AI rewrite buttons (pp. 9-10). Allocated employer accounts: 90,048 (p. 9); distinct people are not reported. The text reports 75% uptake (p. 12, Section 4.1); Table 21 reports 0.752 for 27,111 analyzed records (p. 56), not for every assigned account.

arms.name: Control (status quo)
arms.description: Standard job-posting flow without the platform's AI drafting feature (p. 9). Allocated employer accounts: 90,276 (p. 9); distinct people are not reported. Off-platform AI use is not measured.

participants.exclusions: The unconditional account-level analysis analyzed 180,324 employer accounts (p. 26, Table 3); Figure 12 describes the same experimental sample (p. 55). These are not verified distinct-person counts. Conditional on a first post within 14 days, the word-count analysis analyzed 58,495 posts: 26,781 control and 31,714 treatment (p. 13, Table 1; p. 56, Table 21). Semantic similarity analyzed 32,513 posts (p. 47, Table 12), and the predicted-active-use similarity analysis analyzed 32,282 (p. 18, Table 2); the smaller samples and similarity-analysis arm counts are unexplained. Writing time analyzed 38,203 posts, excluding timed-out or interrupted sessions (p. 13, Table 1). Posting itself responds to treatment, so conditional text contrasts mix composition and drafting effects (p. 24, Section 6).
participants.who: New employer accounts hiring workers on an unnamed online labor market. Population is coded professionals for the hiring activity, not as a claim about the occupation or credentials of the people operating the accounts (p. 7, Section 2).
participants.country: Multinational; Table 20 control percentages are United States 31.34, North America 35.4, South America 1.43, Europe 18.25, Asia 26.82, and Africa 6.52 (PDF p. 55). These are the printed control-arm figures, not whole-sample percentages.
participants.quote: Each employer account is randomized only at their first attempt to create a job post; subsequent attempts keep the same assignment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 9, Section 3; p. 26, Table 3; p. 47, Table 12; pp. 55-56, Figure 12 and Tables 20-21

ai_tool.name_model: Intervention provider/model not stated: 'a popular generative AI service' (p. 10, Section 3.1; footnote 12 is blank). OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 is the measurement model (p. 14, footnote 14; p. 47, Table 12), and GPT4o scores initial-prompt informativeness (p. 48, Figure 10); neither identifies the intervention model.
ai_tool.how_used: A one- or two-sentence prompt produces a full draft plus required skills and category. Employers may freely edit or delete the text, or use the AI's casual, formal, shorten, add-details, and rewrite buttons (pp. 9-10, Section 3.1). The paper states that 66% of these drafts were posted without edits (p. 3); the AI assistance remained available during production.

task.description: Writing the description of the employer's first job post (vacancy advertisement) on the platform; real work, not a lab task.
task.duration: Control mean 8.142 minutes and treatment mean 4.549 minutes among posted jobs written in one sitting; this is observed writing time, not an assigned time limit (PDF p. 13, Table 1; p. 56, Table 21).

outcomes.name: Genericness of posted job descriptions: mean cosine similarity to other posts
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings of final job descriptions; each post is assigned its mean cosine similarity to comparison posts. Higher similarity means less diversity. The comparison pool is described inconsistently (p. 14 versus p. 47). Descending rank is a robustness variant (Table 12); Figure 2 shows the distribution by arm (p. 14), and Figures 13-14 visualize embeddings with PCA (pp. 65, 67). Table 2 gives predicted-active-use subgroup contrasts (p. 18).

contrasts.reported: Direction is reversed for diversity: more similarity means less diversity. Table 12 column (1), GenAI Treatment Assigned: 0.014*** (0.0002); Constant: 0.753*** (0.0002); Observations: 32,513; R2: 0.112. Column (2), descending rank: -6,565.200*** (98.146); Constant: 19,883.000*** (72.941); Observations: 32,513; R2: 0.121. Appendix A.1 states a mean-similarity range of 0.65 to 0.81 and describes the effect as covering 10% of that range. Figure 2 displays the distributions; no standardized effect has been calculated.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 47, Appendix A.1, Table 12; p. 14, Section 4.4 and Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Post-level mean cosine similarity; descending rank is a robustness variant. Larger mean similarity indicates less diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Unresolved. Section 4.4 (p. 14) compares each post with all other posts in its treatment cell; Table 12 notes (p. 47) compare it with all other posts in the experiment. The source does not identify which pool was actually implemented.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Regression on post-level mean-similarity scores, with coefficients and standard errors printed in Table 12 (p. 47). The covariance estimator and any adjustment for dependence between similarity scores are not stated; participant-level precision is not established.
diversity_detail.notes: Conditional on posting; treatment affects posting (p. 24, Section 6). The reason for using 32,513 posts rather than the 58,495 in the word-count analysis is not given (pp. 13, 47). AI availability is an offer, not universal uptake. This is the principal semantic-diversity outcome for an Atlas record, although it is secondary to the paper's stated economic primary outcomes (p. 12). The nonrandomized editing contrast is recorded under S4 and shares this sample.

outcomes.name: Length of job post (number of words)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed word count of the final posted job description (p. 13, Table 1 notes; p. 49, Table 14). The codebook supplies no supported measure code for this mechanical count: automated_score requires a creativity-scoring model or language-model judge, so measure is null. Mean and median regressions and an Anglophone interaction are variants of the same outcome (pp. 13, 49). The application-weighted version analyzes a different observation unit with jobseeker fixed effects: Log Job Post Length coefficient 0.234*** (0.010), with 941,049 applications analyzed (p. 31, Table 6, column 2); it is not an additional independent sample. Standard errors for that application analysis are clustered by jobseeker and job post (p. 30, Section 6.5). Length dispersion is separately recorded as S1-O3.

contrasts.reported: Num Words, treatment coefficient 1.888** (0.801); Constant 94.089*** (0.589); Observations 58,495 (Table 1, column 3). Table 21: control mean 94.089, SD 111.365, median 53.0, n 26,781 posts; treatment mean 95.977, SD 81.804, median 84.0, n 31,714 posts. Table 14, column 3, median contrast 31.000*** (0.563), Constant 53.000*** (0.488). Column 2, Anglophone interaction specification: treatment 1.975* (1.178), Anglophone 5.892*** (1.185), Anglophone X Trt 0.188 (1.606), Constant 90.834*** (0.881); Observations 58,495.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 13, Table 1 column (3); p. 49, Table 14; p. 56, Table 21; p. 51, Figure 11

outcomes.name: Dispersion of job-post length across employers (SD of word count)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Standard deviation of word count within each treatment arm, with the CDF as a graphical representation (p. 13, Section 4.3; p. 51, Figure 11; p. 56, Table 21). This is descriptive dispersion across employers' posts. No creativity-scoring model, AI judge, or lexical-overlap measure is used, and no listed codebook measure fits; measure is null. Unit is set, so n_units does not repeat the number of underlying posts. No inferential test or interval for the SD contrast is reported.

contrasts.reported: Treatment SD 81.804 among 31,714 analyzed posts; control SD 111.365 among 26,781 analyzed posts (Table 21). Section 4.3 rounds these to 82 and 111 words, respectively. Figure 11 plots the CDFs. These are descriptive arm dispersions; no test of the difference in dispersion is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Section 4.3; p. 56, Table 21; p. 51, Figure 11

diversity_detail.computed_over: All posted first job posts within each arm

outcomes.name: Skill count in the job post
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of required skills listed in a job post, an output-detail measure shown in Figure 15(d), conditional on posting (p. 68). Employers can select required skills from a predefined list, and AI can propose required skills (p. 7, Section 2.1; p. 10, Section 3.1). The paper does not establish that the outcome was obtained by manually coding or clustering ideas or categories, as the codebook's category_count definition requires. The measurement procedure and a supported measure code remain unconfirmed, so measure is null. The elaboration/with_ai classification is retained.

contrasts.reported: Figure 15(d): the plotted 95% confidence intervals for both All and Non-Anglo cross zero. No numerical treatment effects, interval endpoints, or output-specific counts are printed.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned the offer of generative-AI drafting at employer-account level (PDF p. 9, Section 3), with assistance available while producing the final job description (p. 10, Section 3.1). Semantic similarity is computed on published text (p. 47, Table 12), satisfying the codebook's writing-across-writers similarity scope and output-scoring criterion. However, the full analysis analyzed 180,324 employer accounts (p. 26, Table 3), and the similarity analysis analyzed 32,513 posts (p. 47, Table 12); neither establishes the number of distinct people analyzed. The complete saved document, including both appendices, provides no account-to-person mapping, so criterion 2 and core eligibility remain unclear. S2 reports no qualifying creativity/diversity outcome (pp. 66, 69-72), and S3 also lacks a verified distinct-person count (p. 68, Figure 15). S4 compares self-selected editors within S1 and remains observational (p. 17, Section 4.5.2; p. 50, Table 15). Setting unsupported word-count, dispersion, and skill-count measure codes to null does not alter the qualifying semantic-similarity outcome.

one_line_finding: Among published job posts, the AI-offer arm had higher mean semantic similarity (coefficient 0.014, SE 0.0002; 32,513 analyzed posts; PDF p. 47, Table 12) and lower word-count dispersion (SD 81.804 versus 111.365; p. 56, Table 21).
open_questions: How many distinct people operated the analyzed employer accounts? A people count or documented account-to-person mapping is needed to settle criterion 2.
Was each post's mean cosine similarity computed within its treatment cell or against all posts in the experiment? Sections 4.4 and A.1/Table 12 conflict.
Why were only 32,513 posts included in Table 12 when the posted-job word-count analysis includes 58,495? Outcome-specific exclusions and arm counts are missing.

How was Figure 15(d)'s skill count constructed? The paper does not establish manual coding or clustering of ideas/categories, so category_count is unconfirmed; this does not affect eligibility through S1 semantic similarity.
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading all 1,463 markdown lines, including both appendices, and checking recorded statistics, counts, and eligibility passages against the 72-page PDF using PyMuPDF text and table extraction. Figure 15 was rendered in memory to confirm directions and whether intervals cross zero; no plotted values were estimated. All locators refer to physical PDF pages, which match printed page numbers. No effect sizes, arm means, missing account totals, or missing person counts were derived. Counts after restriction are described as analyzed. The existing source.supplement description was checked and retained; the internal appendices contain the main similarity coefficients and standard errors. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior audit record; current study fields and final.challenge_resolution supersede its nearest-code measurement conventions. S1-O2, S1-O3, and S3-O1 have null measure codes because mechanical word counts and their descriptive SD do not fit any defined measure code; S3-O2 is null because the skill-count procedure does not establish category_count. The observed outcomes and verified statistics remain recorded. The assignment checker raised no problems. Final counts describe the four corrected outcome-checker problems and one open people-checker evidence gap. S1-S3 retain field_rct design classes, with conditional-on-posting selection noted where relevant. There is no reanalysis of another paper's experiment; S4 compares self-selected editors within S1 and remains observational. Its metric description is limited to mean cosine similarity (p. 50, Table 15); the rank variant belongs to S1 (p. 47, Table 12). Population professionals is a role-based screening classification of hiring activity, not a verified occupation. The paper's primary outcomes are economic; output outcomes remain secondary. Other omitted outcomes concern posting, writing time, applications, hiring, wages, search, screening, and overlap of applicant pools, rather than creativity or diversity of authored text. Prompt/AI-draft quality in Table 13 predicts editing rather than estimating an assistance effect on quality, and jobseekers' cover-letter length concerns people not assigned the drafting assistance. A.8 lacks the example posts promised in footnote 27; no separate data/code or supplement URL is supplied. The unresolved reconciliation difference about S2 counts and the repeated people-count checks are covered by the first final.open_items entry.

open_items.item: Distinct people randomized and analyzed behind S1-S3 employer accounts (open question 1; also the unresolved reconciliation difference for S2 participants.n_randomized). Authors must confirm distinct-person counts or an account-to-person mapping, including the analyzed S1 output sample, to settle criterion 2.

Similarity reference pool (open question 2): Section 4.4 says within treatment cell (p. 14), while Table 12 says all other experimental posts (p. 47). Posted analysis code would identify the implemented pool. Either description scores diversity across outputs, so criterion 3 remains met.

Similarity-sample exclusions and arm counts (open question 3): Table 12 analyzes 32,513 posts versus 58,495 in the word-count analysis (pp. 47, 13). Posted sample-construction data/code would explain exclusions and denominators. This affects extraction and selection assessment; the separate distinct-person-count item covers criterion 2.

Word-count and dispersion measure-code gaps (S1-O2, S1-O3, S3-O1): the observed measures are established, but no current codebook measure label fits. Retain null and the exact descriptions; no additional source is needed to decide eligibility through S1 semantic similarity.

Skill-count construction (new open question): Figure 15(d) does not establish manual coding or clustering of ideas/categories. Author documentation of the procedure would settle whether category_count is supported. This does not affect eligibility through S1 semantic similarity.
